newsitem.title: USA: U.S. debate did little to sway opinions of voters.
newsitem.headline: U.S. debate did little to sway opinions of voters.

text.p: Bob Dole's efforts to tar President Bill Clinton with moral and ethical questions in the final presidential debate did not work, a random sample of public opinion across the country indicated on Thursday.
Buddy Wilson, 45, owner of a Daytona Beach sports bar where half of the TV sets on Wednesday evening were on the Braves-Cardinals baseball game and the other half on the debate, gave this review:

"He let Dole beat himself. What are people going to remember about this? Dole said a lot of bad things about Clinton and Clinton didn't break a sweat. Clinton talked a lot of policy and nobody's going to remember any of that tomorrow, but they'll remember how calm he looked," Wilson said.
Clinton and Dole faced 90 minutes of public questioning on Wednesday in their last face-to-face exchange before the Nov. 5 election.

"I thought it was another sort of draw. Neither one was landing real blows," John Campbell, an agribusiness executive in Omaha, said. "Clinton is so smooth and he can string his sentences together so well ... Dole did a pretty good job but you have to be King Kong to knock Clinton out of this ring.

Karen Matthews, 42, from Daytona Beach, Florida, said: "He (Dole) implied that Clinton was a liar but the things he cited aren't things most people can understand and say 'Yeah, he's right.' Maybe if you're in Congress and you know who's telling the truth, but out here it just sounds like people twisting facts.

"Clinton ignored a lot of what Dole said and that helped him. He kept his answers positive. People want to hear upbeat answers whether it's baloney or not," added Matthews, who said she voted for Clinton in 1992 and was leaning that way again.

In Boston, a 36-year-old accounting manager from Reading, Massachusetts, who asked that his name not be used said he planned to vote for Dole but was disappointed with his performance. "I don't think that Dole answered the questions. I don't think he answered anybody's question. I don't think he did a good job talking and relating to people. I'm not sure he believes that strongly in his points," he said.

Washington lawyer Michele Joy said that when Dole raised ethical issues "Clinton did a nice job of sidestepping and saying we should focus on the future. I think one of the biggest problems is they are too much alike, they're both centrists."

At Mickey's Diner in downtown St. Paul, Minnesota, Mary Kiritschenko, manager-waitress and a Republican, said "Dole better not beat on Clinton too much, that will look embarrassing after the landslide."

In St. Louis, Robin Welch, a temporary employee working at the B. Loehr agency, found the debate "actually kind of boring." Washington University employee Elizabeth Gubser said: "Clinton seemed comfortable ... he didn't do the false schmooze, was very matter-of-fact, which I liked, and poor Dole was kind of in the back carping."

Mary Sullivan, 47, a New York stockbroker who described herself as a staunch Republican, said: "Dole did better than he's ever done before, but Clinton smiles at the camera and everybody believes him."

Maggie Baker, 61, a Houston bank teller, said Dole was wrong to bring up character issues. "The debate should have been focused on what they can do to better the economy and open up more jobs and be sure they can take care of the old and the sick," said Baker, who plans to vote for Clinton.

Troy Godette, a 52-year-old soda delivery man from Silver Spring, Maryland, dismissed Dole's swipe at Clinton's ethics as an 11th-hour "show of desperation ... It seemed like I had heard everything before, so it didn't make any difference."

But Tom Decker, a 44-year-old photocopy technician from Arlington, Vorginia, blasted what he called a trademark "Clintonesque dodging" of the character issue. He said Dole had appeared "more forceful than in the first debate."

New York City school worker Mary Dolan said Clinton "came off as very knowledgeable about the facts. He seems to have legislation right at his fingertips, and I expected Dole to, but he didn't. I thought that Clinton just nailed him."
In Cleveland, an informal survey found that five preferred sleep, baseball or other pursuits to the debate and five others said the event did nothing to change their minds.
